recipe.history:
Bacon's story begins not in a diner or a smokehouse, but in ancient China, where salt-cured pork belly was being preserved as far back as 1500 BCE. The practice spread westward through trade routes, taking root across Europe where different cultures developed their own curing traditions. In Britain, the word 'bacon' came to refer specifically to the back and side cuts of the pig, dry-rubbed with salt and sometimes smoked over wood. By the Roman era, salted pork was a staple of legionary rations — a food built for endurance, for long marches, for survival. Every strip of bacon carries that ancient weight: the knowledge that humans have been coaxing fat and salt and smoke into something transcendent for thousands of years.

Bacon arrived in the American consciousness through the smokehouse traditions of the South and Midwest, where hog farming was central to rural life throughout the 18th and 19th centuries. Pork belly and side cuts, smoked over hickory and applewood, became a breakfast institution. The hamburger, arriving in earnest at American county fairs and lunch counters in the late 1800s, was a natural partner. By the mid-20th century, the bacon cheeseburger had become a cultural landmark — diner menus coast to coast featured it without irony or fanfare, simply because it was correct. The fat from the bacon, rendered and crisped, bastes the beef beneath it. The salt sharpens. The smoke deepens. It is less a topping than a transformation.

This burger takes me back to a specific Saturday morning in my grandmother's kitchen — the sound before the smell, the low spit and crackle of bacon hitting a cold cast iron pan that had been heating for ten minutes. She always started it in a cold pan. Said the fat needed time to introduce itself to the heat. I didn't understand that then. I just understood that the smell that followed was the smell of the weekend, of no school, of time that belonged to me. When I make this burger now, I lay the bacon in cold and wait, the same way she did, and for a moment the kitchen smells like a Saturday that no longer exists except in that specific, irretrievable way that food keeps the past alive.

Cooking a beef patty to medium rare — 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit at the center — is not a preference. It is a position. At that temperature, the myoglobin in the meat has relaxed just enough to release its juices without surrendering them entirely. The fat within the grind has begun to liquefy and marble through the flesh, carrying flavor into every fiber. Cook it further and you are squeezing a sponge dry. A well-formed medium rare patty will resist your thumb with a gentle spring, its center blushing deep rose, its crust seared to a mahogany that concentrates the Maillard reaction into something close to umami perfection. To serve a burger well done is to apologize for the beef. This burger does not apologize.
ingredients: 3 1/2 cups (440g) bread flour, plus more for dusting
3 large eggs, room temperature (2 for dough, 1 for egg wash)
6 tbsp (85g) unsalted butter, softened and cubed
1 lb (450g) freshly ground beef chuck (80/20 lean-to-fat ratio)
1/2 lb (225g) freshly ground beef short rib
8 thick-cut strips (about 1/4 inch) skin-on pork belly or high-quality center-cut bacon
1 cup (240ml) neutral oil (such as grapeseed or canola)
Salt and white pepper to taste
1 medium yellow onion, thinly sliced into rings
2 medium vine-ripened tomatoes, sliced 1/4 inch thick
2 small pickling cucumbers, sliced into 1/4-inch rounds
Flaky sea salt for finishing patty
instructions: 1. MAKE THE QUICK PICKLES (at least 2 hours ahead): Combine vinegar, water, salt, and sugar in a small saucepan over medium heat. Stir until dissolved, then remove from heat. Pack cucumber slices, dill, smashed garlic, peppercorns, and red pepper flakes into a clean jar. Pour hot brine over cucumbers, let cool to room temperature, then seal and refrigerate for at least 2 hours.

2. MAKE THE BRIOCHE BUNS: In a stand mixer bowl, combine warm milk, yeast, and 1 tablespoon of the sugar. Stir gently and let sit 5–10 minutes until foamy. Add the remaining sugar, 2 eggs, and half the flour. Mix on low with the dough hook until just combined.

3. Add the salt and remaining flour, mixing on low until a shaggy dough forms. Increase to medium speed and knead for 5 minutes. With the mixer running, add softened butter one cube at a time, waiting for each piece to fully incorporate before adding the next. This will take about 8–10 minutes. The dough should be smooth, glossy, and slightly tacky.

4. Transfer dough to a lightly oiled bowl, cover with plastic wrap, and let rise at room temperature until doubled, about 1.5 to 2 hours. Alternatively, refrigerate overnight for a slower, more flavorful rise.

5. Punch down dough and turn onto a lightly floured surface. Divide into 4 equal portions (about 130g each). Shape each into a tight ball by pulling the edges underneath and rolling against the counter. Place on a parchment-lined baking sheet, spacing at least 3 inches apart. Flatten slightly to about 1 inch thick. Cover loosely and let proof for 45–60 minutes until noticeably puffed.

6. Preheat oven to 375°F (190°C). Beat remaining egg with 1 tablespoon water. Brush buns gently with egg wash and sprinkle with sesame seeds. Bake 16–19 minutes until deep golden brown. Transfer to a wire rack and cool completely before slicing.

7. CARAMELIZE THE ONIONS: Melt butter in a wide skillet over medium-low heat. Add onion slices with a pinch of salt. Cook, stirring occasionally, for 35–45 minutes until deep golden brown and jammy. Add balsamic vinegar in the last 5 minutes, stir to coat, and cook off the liquid. Set aside.

8. PREPARE AND COOK THE BACON: Preheat oven to 400°F (205°C). Lay bacon strips on a wire rack set over a rimmed baking sheet. Mix brown sugar and smoked paprika; pat mixture onto the top of each strip. Bake 18–22 minutes until rendered, glazed, and deeply caramelized but not brittle — you want some chew. Reserve the drippings from the pan. Let bacon rest on the rack.

9. MAKE THE SMOKED BACON AIOLI: In a medium bowl, whisk together egg yolks, Dijon mustard, and apple cider vinegar until smooth and slightly pale. While whisking constantly, add the neutral oil in an extremely slow, thin stream — drop by drop at first, then a thin drizzle — until the mixture emulsifies and thickens to a creamy mayonnaise. Whisk in smoked paprika, minced garlic, and 1 teaspoon of reserved bacon drippings. Season with salt and white pepper. Refrigerate until needed.

10. FORM THE PATTIES: Combine ground chuck and ground short rib in a bowl. Mix gently with your hands — overworking develops toughness. Divide into 4 equal portions (about 6 oz each). Form each loosely into a ball, then press into a patty approximately 4 inches wide and 3/4 inch thick. Press a shallow dimple in the center of each with your thumb — this prevents the patty from doming as it cooks. Season generously on both sides with kosher salt and black pepper immediately before cooking.

11. COOK THE PATTIES TO MEDIUM RARE: Heat a cast iron skillet or heavy griddle over high heat for 3–4 minutes until smoking. Add no oil — the fat in the grind is sufficient. Place patties dimple-side up in the pan. Do not press. Do not move them. Cook 3 minutes undisturbed until a dark mahogany crust has developed on the bottom.

12. Flip patties once. Immediately lay a slice of white cheddar on each patty. Cook an additional 2–3 minutes. Pull patties at an internal temperature of 130–135°F (54–57°C) measured with an instant-read thermometer inserted through the side of the patty horizontally to the center. Transfer to a clean plate, tent loosely with foil, and rest 3–4 minutes. The carryover will bring the final temp to approximately 133–137°F — a perfect medium rare.

13. TOAST THE BUNS: While patties rest, slice brioche buns in half. Spread cut sides lightly with softened butter. Toast cut-side down in the same skillet over medium heat for 60–90 seconds until golden and slightly crisped at the edges.

14. ASSEMBLE: Spread a generous layer of smoked bacon aioli on both the top and bottom bun. On the bottom bun, layer: lettuce, tomato slices, the rested medium rare patty with melted cheddar, 2 strips of brown sugar bacon crossed over the top, a spoonful of caramelized onions, and a few dill pickle chips. Cap with the top bun, press gently, and finish with a pinch of flaky sea salt over the top if desired. Serve immediately.
